etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French sociable, from Latin sociābilis.

definitions.definition: (of a person) Tending to socialize or be social.

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Society is no comfort to one not sociable.

definitions.definition: Offering opportunities for conversation; characterized by much conversation.
(archaic) Capable of being, or fit to be, united in one body or company; associable.

quote.citation: 1594–1597, Richard Hooker, edited by J[ohn] S[penser], Of the Lawes of Ecclesiastical Politie, […], London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby [for Matthew Lownes], published 1611, →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: They are sociable parts united into one body.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1610, Francis Beaumont, John Fletcher, “Philaster: Or, Love Lies a Bleeding”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1679, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Is the King sociable And bids thee live ?

definitions.definition: (historical) A four-wheeled open carriage with seats facing each other.
A bicycle or tricycle for two persons side by side.
A couch with a curved S-shaped back.
(US) An informal party or church meeting for purposes of socializing.

quote.citation: 1903, George Horace Lorimer, Letters from a Self-Made Merchant to his Son, page 46:
quote.text: At the church sociables he used to hop around among them, chipping and chirping like a dicky-bird picking up seed; and he was a great hand to play the piano, and sing saddish, sweetish songs to them.
